prompt: You prioritise short, predictable start-up, controlled audio callback deadlines and uncomplicated power-off. Which digital approach most naturally supports that design, provided its actual firmware and storage behavior are checked?

options.text: Raspberry Pi with an audio HAT; it costs nothing extra
options.explanation: A general-purpose Linux configuration has an OS boot path and scheduling; writable storage normally needs an orderly shutdown, so it does not naturally give these three properties.

options.text: A bare-metal MCU platform (audio MCU board or MCU plus codec); you give up a full OS, filesystem tools and rich debugging conveniences
options.explanation: Correct. Bare-metal firmware can minimise boot and scheduling complexity. Deadline reliability still requires bounded work, interrupt design and measurement; interrupted non-volatile writes can still corrupt data.

options.text: Any approach, because block size alone determines determinism
options.explanation: Block size sets the deadline, but whether that deadline is met reliably depends on what else can preempt the audio code, which differs between bare metal and a general-purpose OS.

options.text: An analogue synth, because it has no firmware
options.explanation: The project's goals include learning C++ and DSP, and the question concerns the digital approaches. An analogue path changes the project rather than answering it.

workedExample: An MCU can begin its application without booting a full general-purpose OS and can prioritise audio through interrupts. A writable Linux system normally needs an orderly shutdown. Neither headline establishes actual boot time, real-time reliability or immunity to interrupted writes: test the complete selected firmware and storage behavior. The trade-off is doing more platform setup and losing OS conveniences.
